supported_claims.text: 木 is a pictograph of a whole tree: the trunk, branches above, and roots below together depict the physical form. It has no separate phonetic component. The selected oracle-script and bronze-style images are redraws of that tree-like form; the bronze candidate is not tied to a particular dated inscription.

The received Shuowen account describes 木 as growth emerging through the earth and analyzes it as 屮 above a depiction of roots. A paleographic analysis disputes treating 屮 as an independent component, interpreting the graph instead as a complete-body pictograph; this entry follows that whole-tree analysis.

The earliest script evidence reported here includes oracle-bone uses: one interpreted as planting trees and others as a place name and a polity name. The named uses may be proper names or graph loans; no semantic development from ‘tree’ to those names is established.

A Western Zhou bronze inscription is cited for 木枋, interpreted as a wooden writing board. The dossier also records 木 used as a phonetic loan for 沐 in a Mawangdui silk manuscript and in the comparison 木猴/沐猴. These uses do not show a new component or a change in the graph’s pictographic origin.

The graph is used for ‘tree’ and ‘wood/timber’, but the cited dictionary examples generally lack composition dates, so they do not establish when those senses arose or a complete sequence of semantic development. The selected oracle and bronze glyph illustrations are modern vector redraws, not photographs of inscribed artifacts.

disagreements.text: The received Shuowen analysis segments the graph as 屮 with roots below; the paleographic analysis represented in the dossier rejects 屮 as an independent component because resemblance alone does not establish a compound. The latter treats 木 as a whole-tree pictograph.

limitations.text: The oracle-bone examples are reported and interpreted in the dossier, but the underlying rubbings were not inspected. Exact absolute dates for the cited inscriptions and the spoken word’s earliest date are not supplied.

The relation between ‘tree’ and ‘wood/timber’, ‘coffin’, or other listed senses cannot be securely dated or connected from the available dictionary glosses and citations. The chronology and semantic bridges remain unresolved.
The graph’s phonetic loan use for 沐 is documented, but the dossier does not establish an independently dated first occurrence for that borrowing.
